name: range
intent: Represent a span of values as a single interval value whose bound inclusivity and open ends are explicit, so containment and interval-to-interval comparisons live in one place instead of repeated ad-hoc endpoint tests.
problem: Start and end travel together through the code but every caller re-derives what they mean: containment is written as scattered <= / < comparisons that drift apart, "unbounded" is smuggled in as a sentinel value (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31), and interval-to-interval questions - do these two overlap, does one enclose the other, what is the gap between them - have no home at all.
context: Applies wherever a domain concept is a span rather than a point: validity and effectivity periods, booking and availability windows, quantity or price tiers, measurement buckets, version and address ranges, pagination windows, and query parameters such as a date range. It pays off when the same interval is compared repeatedly or crosses a boundary (persistence, API payloads, UI widgets), because the bound convention then has to be written once instead of re-decided per call site. For a single comparison between two local variables the type is pure overhead.
benefits: One owner for bound semantics: inclusive/exclusive choices and the open-end representation are decided in the constructor and honoured by every operation, instead of being re-derived at each call site.
Expressive power that raw pairs lack: open-ended intervals (from x onwards, up to y), empty intervals and all four bound combinations become representable values rather than sentinel endpoints.
Interval-to-interval operations (overlap, encloses, intersection, span, gap/abut) become reusable, nameable and testable in isolation, so callers stop hand-rolling four-comparison overlap tests.
Boundary behaviour becomes explicit: the type is the natural home for the boundary test suite - empty ranges, equal endpoints, adjacent ranges, one-sided ranges - that otherwise never gets written.
Improves the ubiquitous language: Range/Interval/period names the domain concept, so signatures stop carrying ambiguous start/end pairs plus an inclusivity boolean.
Composes with the rest of the model: as an immutable value object the interval can be cached, shared, compared and used as a map key without defensive copies.
tradeoffs: Inclusivity is extra state that every operation must interpret, and structural equality then diverges from set equality: [3..3), (3..3] and (4..4] are all empty yet unequal unless the type canonicalises, which for discrete domains needs domain knowledge (Guava requires a DiscreteDomain).

Open-ended representation is a design decision with no universal answer - a null endpoint versus a plus/minus-infinity special case - and some libraries cannot express it at all (pandas.Interval requires both bounds and left <= right), so a model that needs open ends cannot simply adopt the library type.

Interval-to-interval operations are partial: intersection and gap throw or return null when the ranges are disconnected (Guava throws IllegalArgumentException, Luxon returns null), so callers must pre-test connectedness - the plumbing the pattern promised to remove returns as a precondition.
A dedicated type adds indirection and, in object-oriented languages, an allocation per instance where two primitives would do; in hot loops over primitive bounds this is measurable.

A range is not an index: containment is O(1) but answering "which interval contains x" over many ranges requires an interval tree or sorted container with its own semantics (coalescing, splitting, adjacency), which is a second pattern-sized decision.

In languages without standard-library support (C, Go, JavaScript, TypeScript, and domain-specific C#/Python types) the classic structure must be hand-written, including the well-formedness invariant that the upper endpoint must not precede the lower - easy to skip, and every comparison depends on it.

participants.responsibility: The interval value itself: holds both endpoints, each with its bound kind (closed, open, unbounded), and guarantees the well-formedness invariant so that every operation can assume an ordered pair.

The per-side descriptor of inclusivity - closed (endpoint included), open (excluded) or unbounded (no endpoint on that side) - which keeps the cases explicit instead of encoding them in sentinel values or in a call convention.
Turn intent into a canonical value (closed, closedOpen, open, greaterThan, atMost, all, empty), hiding the bound-kind encoding and the open-end representation from callers.
Domain code that stores intervals (as attributes, collection elements, query parameters) and asks the interval the questions it used to answer with endpoint comparisons.

The structure that holds many intervals and answers point and overlap queries (interval set or map, interval index, range map); it consumes the interval value as its key and adds coalescing, splitting and adjacency policy.

use_cases: Validity and effectivity windows: a contract, price or membership is valid over [effectiveFrom, effectiveTo), and every check is a membership test against one interval.

Booking and availability: a room, seat or resource is reserved during an interval; overlap (not adjacency) decides whether a new booking is possible, and back-to-back bookings must be allowed deliberately.
Quantity and price tiers: the unit price depends on the quantity interval ([1,10), [10,50), [50, +inf)), so a container of intervals with containment lookup replaces a cascade of if-statements.
Temporal queries and reporting: "last 7 days", "this quarter", "since the migration" are half-open or open-ended intervals passed to repositories and rendered by date-range pickers.

Version, port and address ranges: a compatibility claim covers [1.2, 2.0) of a library, a firewall rule covers a port interval - containment answers "is this covered?" and intersection answers "do these rules conflict?".
Pagination and slicing windows: a page is an interval over a sequence, and half-open semantics make adjacency exact ([0,20) followed by [20,40)),

PostgreSQL range and multirange columns: PostgreSQL's daterange, tsrange and numeric range types make lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive bounds, overlap and containment operators, and indexed range queries part of the persistence contract; choose the bound convention before mapping domain intervals.

Guava Range: Java's Guava Range models convex bounded or unbounded intervals with nine open/closed forms, isConnected and intersection; use ContiguousSet only when a discrete domain really requires enumeration rather than treating the interval itself as a sequence.

Standard-library and container choices: Rust's std::ops::RangeBounds covers included, excluded and unbounded bounds when its range forms fit; for many intervals requiring join/split policies, Boost ICL's interval_set and interval_map supply the container semantics instead of overloading one Range value.
avoid_when: Only one comparison exists in one place: comparing two local variables with <= is clearer than introducing a type and a convention.
The "range" is really a set of allowed values with gaps (prime numbers, working days, a list of permitted codes) - a range is convex by definition; use a set or a specification.

The span is a duration without a fixed position on a timeline (3 months, P2D, 90 minutes): a duration or period value is the right concept, and a range needs comparable endpoints (see Quantity for measured amounts).
Containment must be answered over many overlapping intervals at high volume: that is an interval-tree or index problem, so choose the container first and treat the interval value as its key.

The language's standard library already supplies a well-understood range type for exactly this case (Ruby Range, Kotlin IntRange, Swift ClosedRange, Rust std ranges) - use it instead of writing a parallel class.
anti_patterns: Sentinel endpoints standing in for unboundedness (Long.MAX_VALUE for "forever", 0001-01-01 for "always", 9999-12-31 for "end of time"): the sentinel leaks into arithmetic and stops being extreme.

A "Range" that is really an iterable: mixing the interval value with enumeration semantics so the type cannot represent a span over an arbitrary comparable domain or an empty interval (Python's range is exactly the sequence interpretation).
Stringly typed or flag-argument intervals: passing raw start/end pairs plus an "inclusive" string around the code base, so every call site re-decides the comparison and they drift apart.
Endpoint tests re-implemented at each call site (arg.before(start) && arg.after(end) written out several times), the classic source of one site using < where another uses <=.

Declaring half-open semantics but documenting them as closed (or the reverse): the off-by-one-day and off-by-one-item bug, especially where a UI says "1st to 31st" while the API stores [1st, 1st of next month).
Mutable intervals: a range whose endpoints can be reassigned after it was cached, hashed or published, so consumers hold a value that silently changed.
design_principles: Value object: equality by endpoints and bound kinds, no identity, immutable after construction, so intervals can be shared, cached and used as keys.
Encapsulation: the bound-kind encoding (booleans, enums, optionals, infinities) and the open-end representation stay private; clients ask questions, not for fields.
Single responsibility: the interval owns containment and interval-to-interval relations, not formatting, persistence or traversal.
Closure of operations: combining two intervals yields an interval (intersection, span), so composition does not escape into endpoint arithmetic.
Make illegal states unrepresentable: reject an upper endpoint before the lower one in the factory, so every downstream operation can assume order.
Contract-first for partial operations: intersection and gap are defined only for connected or disjoint ranges, so state the precondition and fail fast instead of returning a nonsense value.
best_practices: Settle one representation for open ends (nullable endpoints or a plus/minus-infinity special case) and expose only named factories - greaterThan, atLeast, atMost, lessThan, all, empty - so no caller constructs the encoding by hand.
Document and test the boundaries: empty intervals, single-value intervals, adjacent intervals that must not overlap, and the same set expressed through different bound kinds.

Prefer half-open [start, end) for time and sequences so adjacency is exact, convert at the presentation layer, and state the convention in the type's documentation rather than in a comment at one call site.
Validate in the constructor (ordered endpoints, well-formed bound kinds) and keep the value immutable; derive every other representation from it.
Do not implement interval-to-interval operations on disconnected ranges without a precondition test: expose contains/overlaps/isConnected and let intersection fail fast.
Move many intervals into a container (interval set or map, interval index, range map) instead of looping over a list, and pick its coalescing or splitting policy deliberately.
Keep a canonical form for discrete domains when intervals are compared, deduplicated or used as keys, because [1,2) and [1,1] are the same integer set but not the same value.
sources: Martin Fowler, Range (eaaDev draft, 7 March 2004) - a single object representing a range of values, with bound inclusivity for continuous types, open-ended ranges handled by null endpoints or Special Case extremes, and the operations includes, overlaps, abuts and gap. https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/Range.html

Martin Fowler, Analysis Patterns: Reusable Object Models (Addison-Wesley, 1997) - the Range model with isLowerInclusive/isUpperInclusive flags and includes/overlaps/abuts operations (slide deck: https://www.scribd.com/document/435524971/MartinFowlerAnalysisPatterns-pdf).

PostgreSQL Documentation, Range/Multirange Functions and Operators. https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-range.html
